mainTopic: Wine that can't be drunk, and when a promise to pay a rescuer for his loss is binding: 'I was joking,' the ferry case, the donkeys in the river, and rescues that end unexpectedly.
overview: This amud opens at the end of a ברייתא about wine that cannot be drunk. בית שמאי say to pour it out, and בית הלל say it may be used for sprinkling. רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי offers a compromise, reported in two versions, but the חכמים reject it: a third opinion cannot decide. The גמרא then returns to our משנה. It asks why the honey owner must keep his promise to pay for the wine, instead of saying 'I was joking,' as an escaping prisoner may say to a ferryman. The answer is that the honey case matches the second half of the ferry ברייתא, where the ferryman is a fisherman who lost real income. Next, the גמרא explains why the משנה needs both the wine case and the donkey case. רב rules that a rescuer whose own donkey came out of the river by itself still collects, which is compared to the story of רב ספרא and the lion. רבי rules that a rescuer who failed gets only his wage, and רב begins a challenge from a ברייתא about hiring a worker, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Pour it all out vs. use it for sprinkling
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends בית שמאי's view (pour out all the wine) and gives בית הלל's view (use it for sprinkling).
steps.simpleTranslation: [בית שמאי say:] It must all be poured out. And בית הלל say: Let it be used for sprinkling.
steps.whatsHappening: We are in the middle of a ברייתא. בית שמאי say the wine that can't be drunk must be poured out, and בית הלל say it can be sprinkled around for its smell.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בית שמאי worry that if the wine is kept around, someone might end up drinking it, so they want it destroyed. בית הלל allow a use that gets some benefit from the wine without drinking it.

keyTerms.meaning: It must all be poured out
Sprinkling (spraying wine for its pleasant smell)

phrases.english: it must all be poured out,
and Beit Hillel say:
let it be used for sprinkling.
phrases.notes: Sprinkling means spraying the wine around a room for its nice smell, instead of drinking it.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: pour out all the wine. בית הלל: it may be used for sprinkling.

steps.title: A middle position: house vs. field
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי decides between them: in the house the wine may be sprinkled, and in the field it must be poured out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי said: I will decide between them. In the house, let it be used for sprinkling. In the field, it must all be poured out.
steps.whatsHappening: A third תנא offers a compromise that splits the case by location.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the house the wine can be sprinkled right away, so there is little risk that someone drinks it. In the field it would have to be carried home first, and on the way someone might drink it, so it must be poured out.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, said:
I will decide [between them];
in the house – let it be used for sprinkling,
and in the field – it must all be poured out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי: אֲנִי אַכְרִיעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a compromise between the two views in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the house: sprinkle. In the field: pour it all out.

steps.title: Another version: aged vs. new wine
steps.stepSummary: Others report that his compromise was really between aged wine (may be sprinkled) and new wine (must be poured out).
steps.simpleTranslation: There are those who say: With aged wine, let it be used for sprinkling. With new wine, it must all be poured out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי's compromise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Aged wine already has a good smell, so it can be sprinkled right away. New wine does not smell nice yet and would sit around waiting, which risks someone drinking it, so it must be poured out.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say (another version)

phrases.english: There are those who say:
phrases.notes: This is another version of what רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי said.

phrases.english: with aged [wine] – let it be used for sprinkling,
and with new [wine] – it must all be poured out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second report of the same compromise, using a different dividing line.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Aged wine: sprinkle. New wine: pour it all out.

steps.title: A third opinion cannot decide
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים reject his compromise: a third opinion cannot settle a dispute between two others.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: A third decision does not decide.
steps.whatsHappening: The other חכמים push back against רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי's attempt to settle the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A compromise that takes a little from each side is just a new, third opinion. It does not count as deciding between בית שמאי and בית הלל.
steps.whatToRemember: בית שמאי say pour it out, בית הלל say sprinkle, and the middle-ground compromise is rejected because 'a third decision does not decide.'

phrases.english: They said to him:
A third decision does not decide.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אֵין הַכְרָעָה שְׁלִישִׁית מַכְרַעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the compromise from steps 2–3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole compromise, in either version.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A third opinion cannot settle a dispute between two other opinions.

steps.title: Why can't he say 'I was joking'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling that a promise to pay for the wine is binding, and asks why the honey owner can't claim he was only joking.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The משנה says:] If he said to him, 'I will save yours, and you pay me for mine,' he must pay. Why? Let him say to him: 'I was joking with you!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to our משנה and challenges its ruling that the honey owner must pay the full value of the wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The honey owner agreed to the deal under pressure, while his honey was spilling. So why can't he later say he never really meant it? This kind of claim seems like it should cancel the promise.

phrases.english: If he said to him:
'I will save yours, etc.'
phrases.notes: Quoting the משנה: the wine owner pours out his wine to save his friend's honey, on condition he gets paid for his wine.

phrases.english: Why?
Let him say to him:
'I was joking with you!'

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמַּאי? וְנֵימָא לֵיהּ: מְשַׁטֶּה אֲנִי בָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic: back to the משנה about the wine and the honey.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the honey owner must pay the full value of the wine.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A promise made under pressure should be cancellable with the claim 'I was joking with you.'

steps.title: The escaping prisoner and the ferry
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: a prisoner who promised a ferryman a דינר to take him across pays only the normal fare.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it taught: If someone was fleeing from prison and a ferry was in front of him, and he said to the ferryman, 'Take a דינר and bring me across,' the ferryman gets only his usual fare.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support its challenge. This sets up the comparison in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here a person promised far more than the usual price while he was desperate, and the ברייתא says he does not have to pay it. This seems to show that a promise made under pressure is not binding.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it taught in a ברייתא?

phrases.english: Isn't it taught in a baraita:
where one was fleeing from prison
and there was a ferry before him,
he said to him: 'Take a dinar and bring me across' –
he has only his [usual] wage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to back up the challenge in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That a promise made under pressure can be cancelled.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the prisoner and the ferryman.

steps.title: Applying the ferry case to the honey
steps.stepSummary: From the ferry case we see a person can say 'I was joking.' So the honey owner should be able to say it too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Apparently the prisoner can say to him, 'I was joking with you.' Here too, let the honey owner say, 'I was joking with you!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the lesson from the ברייתא and uses it to sharpen its question on the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only reason the prisoner pays just the usual fare is that he can say 'I was joking.' Both cases involve a promise made in a moment of need, so the honey owner should be able to make the same claim. This puts the משנה's ruling into direct tension with the ברייתא.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not ruling that the honey owner is exempt. It is only asking why the משנה makes him pay. The next step answers this.

phrases.english: Apparently he can say to him:
'I was joking with you';
here too, let him say to him:
'I was joking with you!'

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא אָמַר לֵיהּ: מְשַׁטֶּה אֲנִי בָּךְ; הָכָא נָמֵי, לֵימָא לֵיהּ: מְשַׁטֶּה אֲנִי בָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the inference from the ברייתא in step 6 and applies it to the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the honey owner must pay the full value of the wine.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ferry ברייתא lets a pressured promiser say 'I was joking,' so the honey owner should be able to say it too.

steps.title: The honey case matches the second half of the ferry ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The honey case is not like the first half of the ferry ברייתא, where only the normal fare is paid. It is like the second half, where the full דינר is paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: This case is not like that one. It is like the second half of the ברייתא: if he said, 'Take this דינר as your pay and bring me across,' he pays him the full amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 7. It says the wine-and-honey case should be compared to a different part of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ferry ברייתא has two halves. In the first, the passenger pays only the regular fare. In the second, he pays the full דינר. The honey case matches the second half, so the promise is binding and 'I was joking' does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter (second) clause of a source

steps.confusionAlert: Both halves of the ferry ברייתא involve a promise of a דינר. The difference between them is not yet explained here. The גמרא asks about it in the next step.

phrases.english: This is not comparable, except to the latter clause
phrases.notes: He means the honey case is like the second half of the ferry ברייתא, not the first half.

phrases.english: And if he said to him:
'Take this dinar as your wage,
and take me across'
he gives him his wage in full.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7 by pointing to the other half of the same ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-matching the comparison to a different clause of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The honey case is like the ferry case where only the normal fare is paid, so the owner could say 'I was joking.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The honey case is like the second half, where the full promised amount is paid.

steps.title: What is the difference between the two halves of the ferry ברייתא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the first half gives only the normal fare while the second half gives the full דינר.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about the first half, and what is different about the second half?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question. It sets up the next step, which will explain the difference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both halves seem to be the same promise of a דינר for a ride across the river. Until we know what separates them, the answer in step 8 is not fully clear.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of a source

phrases.english: What is different about the first clause
and what is different about the latter clause?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא רֵישָׁא וּמַאי שְׁנָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the distinction used in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the second half of the ferry ברייתא gives the full amount and the first half does not

steps.title: The second half is about a fisherman who lost real income
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא explains that the second half is about a fisherman. He can say, 'You made me lose fish worth a זוז.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: The second half is about a fisherman who catches fish from the sea. He can say to the passenger, 'You made me lose a זוז worth of fish.'
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא answers the question. The ferryman in the second half is a fisherman who stopped fishing to give the ride, so he really lost money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The full דינר is binding because it pays back a real loss, not just the job of rowing. The wine owner in the משנה is similar. He really lost his wine to save the honey, so the honey owner's promise to pay is binding.

keyTerms.meaning: Who scoops out or draws up
A זוז, a coin worth the same as a דינר

steps.whatToRemember: A promise to pay more than the normal price is binding when it pays back a real loss. That is why the honey owner must pay for the wine.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the rule for the wine case. Whoever gives up his own property to save someone else's, after being promised payment, gets paid back in full.

phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama said:
It is speaking of a trapper who scoops fish from the sea,
and he can say to him:
You made me lose fish worth a zuz.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The second half is about a fisherman who lost real income, so the full promised amount pays back a true loss.

steps.title: Quoting the donkey case from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next case in the משנה: a river swept away two donkeys, and one is worth a מנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: A river swept away his donkey and his friend's donkey. His donkey was worth a מנה, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new section by quoting the donkey case from the משנה. This sets up a discussion of why the משנה needs this case as well as the wine case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, a person leaves his own donkey to save his friend's more valuable one. The case is close to the wine-and-honey case, so the גמרא is about to ask why both were taught.

keyTerms.meaning: A מנה, a sum of one hundred דינרים
Etc., the quote continues in the משנה

phrases.english: A river swept away his donkey and the donkey of his fellow,
his is worth a maneh, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic by quoting the next case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's donkey case, cited to begin discussing it

steps.title: Why the wine case alone would not be enough
steps.stepSummary: Both cases are needed. From the wine case alone, we might think full payment applies only because the wine owner actively spilled his wine. A donkey that drowns on its own might give only a wage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both cases are needed. If the משנה taught only the first case, I would say: only there, when he made a deal, does he get the full value, because he destroyed his wine with his own hands. But here the donkey is lost by itself, so I would say he gets only his wage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה needs both cases. It starts by showing what we would get wrong if we had only the wine case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the wine case, the owner pours out his own wine. That is a direct, active loss. In the donkey case, the river carries the donkey away on its own. So we might think the rescuer deserves only payment for his work, even if he made a deal.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary, both cases are needed
With his own hands, an active loss

phrases.english: And it is necessary;
for if it had taught us only the first case,
it is there that, when he stated it explicitly,
phrases.notes: 'Stated it explicitly' means he made clear he wanted to be paid back for his loss.

phrases.english: he gives him the value of all of it,
because he is losing it with his own hands;
but here, where it is lost by itself,
let us say: he has only his wage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins explaining why the donkey case in step 11 is needed alongside the wine case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wine case alone would not teach that a stipulated loss is repaid in full when the loss happens by itself.

steps.title: Why the donkey case alone would not be enough, so both are needed
steps.stepSummary: From the donkey case alone, we might think the wine owner gets full value even without making a deal, since his loss is active. So both cases are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the משנה taught only the second case, I would say: only here, when nothing was said, does he get just his wage, because the donkey was lost by itself. But there, where he destroyed his wine with his own hands, I would say he gets the full value even if nothing was said. So both cases are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining why both cases are needed. It shows the mistake we would make if we had only the donkey case, then concludes that both are necessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the donkey case, without a deal the rescuer gets only his wage. But the wine owner actively destroyed his property, so we might think he gets full value even without a deal. The wine case teaches that without a deal he too gets only his wage, so each case adds something.

keyTerms.meaning: When nothing was said, with no deal made
I would say, the mistaken thought
The value of all of it

steps.whatToRemember: The rule is the same in both cases. With a clear deal, the rescuer gets the full value of his loss. Without one, he gets only a wage. Active loss or passive loss makes no difference.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two halves. The first half (step 12) is about a case where he made a deal. This half is about a case where he made no deal (בסתמא). Each case on its own would lead to a different mistake.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only the latter case,
it is here that when nothing was specified
he has only his wage,
because it is lost by itself;
but there, where it is with his own hands,
I would say that even when nothing was specified
he gives him the value of all of it;
it is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the explanation begun in step 12 and concludes that both cases are needed.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both the wine case and the donkey case are needed. Together they teach that full repayment depends on making a deal, not on whether the loss was active or happened by itself.

steps.title: What if the rescuer's own donkey came out by itself?
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא asks רב about a rescuer who went to save his friend's donkey, but his own donkey climbed out of the river on its own.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא asked רב: A man went down to save his friend's donkey, and his own donkey came up out of the river by itself. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new question about the משנה's donkey case. The rescuer made a deal to be paid for his own donkey, but his own donkey was not lost after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The deal was meant to pay him back for losing his own donkey. Now he lost nothing. So the question is whether he can still collect the full value of his donkey from his friend.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him (a question to a teacher)
He went down to save (the other donkey)

phrases.english: Rav Kahana asked Rav:
If he went down to rescue,
phrases.notes: He went into the river to save his friend's donkey instead of his own, after making a deal to be paid back.

phrases.english: and his own came up by itself, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the donkey case of the משנה and asks about a new twist.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the rescuer still collect his donkey's value if his donkey survived on its own?

steps.title: Heaven showed him mercy, so he still gets paid
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that the rescuer still collects, because his donkey surviving was a gift from Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to him: From Heaven they had mercy on him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question. The rescuer still gets the full payment he was promised.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rescuer gave up his donkey when he went to save his friend's. That his donkey came out alive is his own good luck from Heaven. It does not cancel his friend's promise to pay.
steps.whatToRemember: If the rescuer gave up his donkey and it survived anyway, he still collects what he was promised. His good luck belongs to him.

phrases.english: He said to him: From Heaven they had mercy on him.
phrases.notes: He means the rescuer still gets paid. The survival of his donkey is a gift to him, not to his friend.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rescuer still collects the promised payment. His donkey's survival is Heavenly mercy for him.

steps.title: The story of רב ספרא, the lion and the caravan
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tells a similar story. רב ספרא gave his donkey to a lion as his turn, the lion did not eat it, and רב ספרא took it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like the story of רב ספרא. He was traveling in a caravan, and a lion followed them. Every night the travelers sent the lion one person's donkey, and the lion ate it. When רב ספרא's turn came, he sent his donkey, but the lion did not eat it. רב ספרא went ahead and took ownership of it again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story that matches רב's answer. רב ספרא did his share for the group, but his donkey was saved anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the rescuer, רב ספרא fully gave up his donkey. The lion not eating it was Heaven's kindness to him, so he could keep it. His duty to the group was already done.

keyTerms.meaning: A caravan, a group of travelers

phrases.english: Like this case of Rav Safra:
he was traveling in a caravan,
a certain lion followed along with them.
Every night they would throw to it
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets is in the printed גמרא. The word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

phrases.english: the donkey of one of them, and it would eat it.
When Rav Safra's turn came,
he threw his donkey to it, and it did not eat it.
Rav Safra went ahead and took ownership of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows a real story that matches רב's idea in step 15.
steps.raayaObject: רב's rule that a person's lucky escape from loss does not cancel what he already did.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב ספרא gave his donkey as his turn. The lion did not eat it, and he kept it.

steps.title: Why did רב ספרא need to take the donkey again?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדיפתי asks רבינא why רב ספרא had to acquire his donkey again, since he only gave it up for the lion.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא מדיפתי said to רבינא: Why did he need to acquire it? True, he gave it up. But he gave it up only for the lion. He did not give it up for everyone!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions one detail in the story: רב ספרא taking the donkey back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא argues that the donkey never became ownerless for other people. It was given up only so the lion could eat it. So nobody else could take it, and it still belonged to רב ספרא without any new act of taking.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּיפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha of Difti said to Ravina:
Why did he need to acquire it?
Granted that when he made it ownerless,
he made it ownerless with the lion in mind,
he did not make it ownerless for everyone!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּיפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא: לְמָה לֵיהּ לְמִיזְכֵּי בֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges one action in the story of step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ספרא's act of acquiring his donkey again.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The הפקר was limited to the lion, so the donkey stayed his, and acquiring it again was pointless.

steps.title: רב ספרא was just being extra careful
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that רב ספרא acquired the donkey only as an extra safety step.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to him: רב ספרא did it just to be extra careful.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the question. He agrees the act was not truly needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא does not argue with רב אחא's reasoning. He explains that רב ספרא acted out of extra caution, in case the הפקר had worked for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: To be extra careful, for added safety

phrases.english: He said to him: Rav Safra
did it to be extra careful.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: רַב סָפְרָא לְרַוְוחָא דְמִילְּתָא הוּא דַּעֲבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts the point but explains the act as extra caution.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב ספרא's act seemed to show that the donkey became ownerless for everyone.
steps.terutzMaskana: The act was only an extra safety step. It was not strictly needed.

steps.title: What if he tried to rescue but failed?
steps.stepSummary: רב asks רבי about a man who went down to save his friend's donkey but did not manage to save it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב asked רבי: A man went down to save his friend's donkey, but he did not save it. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second question about the משנה's donkey case. This time the rescue did not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the rescuer may have lost his own donkey, and his friend gained nothing. The question is whether the friend must still pay for the rescuer's donkey.

keyTerms.meaning: And he did not save it

phrases.english: Rav asked Rabbi:
If he went down to rescue but did not rescue, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question on the same משנה case, about a failed rescue.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the friend still pay the full value of the rescuer's donkey if the rescue failed?

steps.title: A failed rescuer gets only his wage
steps.stepSummary: רבי answers that this is an obvious case: he gets only his wage, not the value of his donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי said to him: Is this a question? He gets only his wage.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי answers that the answer is obvious. The failed rescuer gets paid only for his effort.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The friend promised to pay for the rescuer's donkey in exchange for saving his own donkey. Since nothing was saved, the friend owes only a basic wage for the work.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this a question? (It is obvious.)
His wage, pay for his work

steps.whatToRemember: If his own donkey survives, the rescuer still collects the full promised value (רב). If the rescue fails, he gets only a wage (רבי).
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. In step 15 the rescue worked and he got lucky, so he collects in full. Here the rescue failed, so he gets only a wage.

phrases.english: He said to him: Is this a question?
He has only his wage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A rescuer who failed gets only his wage, not the value of his own donkey.

steps.title: רב begins a challenge from a teaching about hiring a worker
steps.stepSummary: רב raises an objection to רבי's ruling and starts quoting a ברייתא that opens with the case of someone who hires a worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב challenged רבי from a ברייתא: In the case of someone who hires a worker...
steps.whatsHappening: רב is starting to challenge רבי's answer from Step 20. This line only sets up the challenge: it gives the opening words of the ברייתא, and the rest of the source comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אֵיתִיבֵיהּ tells us a challenge from an earlier teaching is coming. The ברייתא is about a hired worker, and רב will use it to question רבי's ruling that the failed rescuer gets only his wage. We have to wait for the rest of the ברייתא to see exactly how it clashes.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection to him, usually by quoting an earlier source

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the whole challenge yet. Only the first words of the ברייתא are quoted here, so don't try to figure out the contradiction until you see the rest.

phrases.english: He raised an objection to him: One who hires a worker
phrases.notes: רב is challenging רבי's ruling from Step 20. The quoted teaching keeps going after these words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a challenge against רבי's answer in Step 20, which said the failed rescuer gets only his wage.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's ruling that one who tried to save his friend's donkey and failed receives only his wage
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב brings a ברייתא about a hired worker, which he will use to question רבי's ruling. The full argument depends on the rest of the ברייתא, which continues next.
